name: Reverse Prompt Engineering (RPE) — Genetic-Algorithm Black-Box Inversion
executive_summary: Reconstruct an unknown prompt from as few as 5 outputs, with no model access beyond querying it: an LLM proposes candidates, a genetic algorithm evolves them by how closely their outputs match the target.
description: Frames prompt reconstruction as a black-box optimization problem: given a small set of outputs produced by an unknown latent prompt, an LLM (acting as both candidate-generator and mutation operator) proposes candidate prompts, each candidate is scored by feeding it back through the target LLM and measuring output similarity to the real observed outputs, and a genetic-algorithm-style loop (selection, crossover, mutation) evolves the population toward candidates whose outputs best match. Unlike prior inversion methods (logit2prompt, output2prompt) that require training a dedicated T5-based recovery model, large numbers of output examples, or access to output logits, RPE requires no training, no logits, and as few as 5 text outputs — making it applicable to closed-source, API-only LLMs. Reports outperforming output2prompt by an average 5.1-9.5% in cosine similarity across models, and produces coherent natural-language prompts rather than the garbled text earlier methods sometimes yield.
when_to_use: Security auditing of a deployed LLM application — assessing how easily its hidden system prompt could be reconstructed by an attacker who can only see outputs.
Recovering or adapting a prompt behind an output you want to reuse or repurpose, when only the output (not the original prompt) is available.
when_not_to_use: The target model's outputs are truly logit/probability-inaccessible AND extremely limited (fewer than ~5 examples) — reconstruction quality degrades with too little signal.
A white-box audit is possible instead (model weights/gradients available) — SODA-style exact inversion is more precise when that access exists.
known_pitfalls: Recovers a prompt that is functionally/semantically similar enough to reproduce the outputs, not necessarily the exact original wording — treat the output as a high-quality reconstruction, not a guaranteed verbatim recovery.

usage_templates.template:
# Inputs: observed target outputs A = {{observed_outputs}} from an unknown prompt p, produced by target model {{target_llm}}

# Initialize population
Using an LLM, propose {{population_size}} distinct candidate prompts that could plausibly have produced outputs like: {{observed_outputs}}

# Per generation (repeat up to {{max_generations}} times)
For each candidate prompt in the population, query {{target_llm}} with it and compare the resulting output(s) to {{observed_outputs}} using distance metric {{similarity_metric}} (e.g. cosine similarity of embeddings).
Select the top-scoring candidates, then use the LLM to produce the next generation via crossover (combine elements of two high-scoring candidates) and mutation (rephrase/vary one high-scoring candidate).

# Output
Return the highest-scoring candidate across all generations as the reconstructed prompt p'.

variables.name: observed_outputs
variables.description: The small set of real outputs produced by the unknown target prompt

variables.name: target_llm
variables.description: The black-box model being queried (only text outputs are needed, not logits)

variables.name: population_size
variables.description: How many candidate prompts per generation

variables.name: max_generations
variables.description: Generation budget for the genetic algorithm

variables.name: similarity_metric
variables.description: Distance/similarity function comparing candidate output to observed output

usage_templates.reproducibility_note: This template intentionally samples multiple times or explores adaptively; outputs vary run to run by design (explicit temperature>0 sampling, or multi-branch search whose path depends on intermediate stochastic choices).
